lines: ### Fixed

+- **A malformed save is now refused at the door instead of crashing the engine**: `parseSave` — the one seam every save reader shares — documented itself as _total_ ("unknown shapes … all yield null") but only checked that the top-level `changes` and `players` were **arrays**, never what was in them. So a current-version save like `{version: 18, seed: 1, changes: [1], players: [null]}` passed validation and then threw deeper in, where nothing is defensive by design: the engine's constructor does `save.players.find((p) => p.id === …)` on the null, and `applySavedChanges` destructures every change as a tuple. It now validates entries — player entries must be objects with a string id, changes must be `[index, blockId]` integer pairs, and a `dimensions` section must carry a usable `changes` array. Malformed **entries drop** (one bad pair must not cost you your world — matching every other reader in the module, which has always dropped rather than thrown), while a malformed **save** still reads as no save. Block ids are bounded to the voxel array's 0–255 storage width, since a larger id wouldn't fail loudly — it would wrap (`300 & 255` = 44) and silently become a _different real block_ — but they're deliberately not allow-listed against `BlockId`, because a hand-maintained ceiling would silently discard legitimate blocks the day someone appends an id and forgets to raise it, trading a cosmetic failure (unknown ids already render magenta) for real data loss. Deep per-field validation stays where it already lives, in the restorers. Separately, the **cloud download** was the one save path that skipped all of this — it cast the decompressed JSON straight to `SaveData`, so a corrupt blob rode into the engine — and now validates like the rest; anything that isn't a save reads as "no save here", which the callers already treat as "keep what's local".

- **An invited player can no longer overwrite a multiplayer world's authoritative save**: `sp-cloud` and `mp` worlds keep their save in the same `worlds.saveBlob` column, but they don't share its ownership — an `sp-cloud` blob **is** the client's upload, while an `mp` blob is the game server's authoritative persistence, which a room reloads as world state on its next boot. `PUT /api/worlds/:id/save` gated on membership but never on `kind`, so anyone holding an invite could upload a crafted `SaveData` over a shared world and have the server adopt it wholesale on the next room boot — inventories, builds, the lot — bypassing the server authority the protocol reserves for itself ("clients cannot invent items or edits", [docs/protocol.md](docs/protocol.md#trust-model)). Nothing legitimate ever uploaded an `mp` world (the in-game push returns early when online, and mp worlds carry no `cloudId`), so uploads are now `sp-cloud`-only — the mirror image of the `mp`-only check the join-ticket path already made. Reads stay membership-gated: a member can already see the world by playing it. Separately, the upload route now rejects an oversized body on its declared `content-length` before buffering it, and stored blobs inflate through a bounded gunzip (gzip runs ~1000:1 on hostile input, so an unbounded inflate turns a few MiB of stored bytes into GiB of heap on a 512 MB VM) — with the kind gate in place a room should only ever read blobs it wrote itself, so that bound is defense in depth rather than a live vector, but it's the seam where stored bytes become engine state and shouldn't trust the row on the far side.

git add -A && git commit -F- <<'EOF'
fix(save): make save decoding total at every seam

parseSave's own docstring promised totality — "unknown shapes, future
versions, and migration throws all yield null" — but it only checked
that `changes` and `players` were arrays, never what was inside them. So
this passed validation and then threw deeper in:

    { version: 18, seed: 1, changes: [1], players: [null] }

Nothing downstream is defensive about that, by design: parseSave is the
seam that guarantees shape, so the engine's ctor does
`save.players.find((p) => p.id === …)` on the null, and
applySavedChanges destructures `const [idx, block] of changes` on the 1.
Both throw. This restores the contract the code already claimed rather
than inventing a new one.

Validated: player entries are objects with a string id; changes are
[index, blockId] pairs of non-negative integers; a `dimensions` section
carries a usable `changes` array (dimensionSectionOf hands whatever it
finds straight to applySavedChanges, so `{ nether: {} }` threw at the
for-of).

Entries are DROPPED, not fatal — one bad pair must not cost a player
their world, and every sibling reader in this module (mobs, vehicles,
containers, effects, stats) already drops-not-throws. A malformed *save*
(no seed, no players array, unknown version) still reads as no save.

Two deliberate non-changes, against what the review asked for:

- Per-field validation stays in the restorers. restoreMobs,
  restoreVehicles, readContainers, readLootedChests, restoreEffects and
  restoreStats are ALREADY total per-entry — allow-listed ids, finite
  checks, the lot. Re-validating those fields here would duplicate them
  and give the save format two places to disagree about what a player
  is. The gap was never the fields; it was the entries holding them.

- Block ids are bounded to 0–255 but NOT allow-listed against BlockId.
  The bound is real: the voxel array is a Uint8Array, so 300 would not
  fail loudly, it would wrap to 44 and silently become a different real
  block. But BlockId is a const enum (nothing to enumerate at runtime),
  and a hand-maintained ceiling would silently discard legitimate blocks
  the day someone appends an id and forgets to raise it — trading a
  cosmetic failure (an unknown id already renders magenta via
  BLOCK_COLORS[block] ?? [1,0,1]) for real data loss. 0–255 is the
  storage width, not a list to keep in sync.

Also routes the cloud download through parseSave. It cast decompressed
JSON straight to SaveData — the only save path skipping validation,
while the server's load path has always gone through readSave. Doing so
immediately caught a test fixture that was not a valid save (no
`players`): it had only ever "worked" because the cast hid it.

Regression pinned end-to-end in GameEngine.test.ts, not just at the
parser: the reported object now boots a world. Verified it does throw
without the fix.
EOF
git log --oneline -1

**Commit 3 is in (`03caea4`).** Full suite 1514 pass, exit 0.

The interesting part was scoping it *down*. Codex asked me to validate "tuples, objects, block identifiers, coordinates, array lengths, numeric ranges" across `blockEntities`, `mobs`, `vehicles`, `lootedChests`, and `dimensions`. But `restoreMobs`, `restoreVehicles`, `readContainers`, `readLootedChests`, `restoreEffects`, and `restoreStats` are **already total per-entry** — allow-listed ids, finite checks, the lot. Doing what was asked would have duplicated well-tested code and given the save format two places to disagree about what a player is. The gap was never the fields; it was the *entries* holding them. So `parseSave` now guarantees structure, and the restorers keep owning per-field validation.

I also declined the block-id allow-list, for a reason worth knowing: `BlockId` is a `const enum`, erased at runtime, so there's nothing to enumerate. A hand-maintained ceiling would silently discard legitimate blocks the day someone appends id 101 and forgets to raise it — trading a *cosmetic* failure (unknown ids already render magenta) for real data loss. I did bound ids to 0–255, because that's the Uint8Array's actual storage width: `300` doesn't fail loudly, it wraps to `44` and silently becomes a different real block.

Two things fell out that codex didn't report. Routing the cloud download through `parseSave` immediately caught a **test fixture that wasn't a valid save** — it lacked `players`, and had only ever passed because the bare cast hid it. And a `dimensions: { nether: {} }` section throws at `applySavedChanges`'s `for...of`, a third crash path alongside the two reported.

I verified the reported crasher genuinely throws without the fix and boots a world with it, so the regression test in `GameEngine.test.ts` pins the actual symptom rather than just the parser.

Next is commit 4 — `saveRevision`. It carries the migration and can't be split, so it's the most delicate one in the branch.

-- Split the save cursor out of the metadata mtime.
--
-- "updated_at" was doing two jobs: metadata mtime (list ordering) and the save
-- revision every device compares to decide whether the cloud moved. Renaming a
-- world bumped it, so every other device's cursor went stale over a save that
-- had not changed — their next push 409'd and the client latched cloud sync off
-- for the session. "save_revision" now counts blob writes and nothing else.
--
-- The backfill is load-bearing. save_revision = 0 means "never saved", which is
-- what putSaveBlob checks to accept a first upload. Existing worlds that ALREADY
-- hold a blob must therefore start at 1, or a client with no cursor would be
-- treated as a first upload and clobber a real save. Worlds with no blob keep
-- the 0 default.
--
-- Deploy order: this migration is additive and safe to run before the app ships
-- (an old build simply ignores the column). The web app and the game server both
-- write save_revision, so they must ship TOGETHER — see docs/deploy.md.
ALTER TABLE "worlds" ADD COLUMN "save_revision" integer DEFAULT 0 NOT NULL;--> statement-breakpoint
UPDATE "worlds" SET "save_revision" = 1 WHERE "save_blob" IS NOT NULL;

concurrency: each device sends the `updatedAt` stamp it last saw

input.new_string:
Single-player cloud saves are gzipped `SaveData` blobs (`lib/game/
cloudSaves.ts` — block diffs compress extremely well) with last-write-wins
concurrency: each device sends the `saveRevision` it last saw
(`x-base-revision`); a mismatch is **409** and the pushing client stops
syncing and warns (rather than clobber the other device), then adopts the
newer save on the next open.

**Two clocks, deliberately.** `worlds.updatedAt` is metadata mtime — "last
touched", what the world list orders by. `worlds.saveRevision` counts **blob
writes and nothing else**: it is the sync cursor devices compare (stored per
world under `minecraft_cloud_stamps_v2`) and the CAS token their uploads race
on, incremented SQL-side by both writers (`putSaveBlob` and the game server's
`storeWorld`) so concurrent writes can't settle on a value read earlier.
Revision `0` means never saved, which is what makes "first upload" checkable
without trusting the client. They must stay separate: while `updatedAt` served
as both, **renaming a world moved every other device's cursor** and 409'd its
next push over a save that hadn't changed — and since a 409 latches
`cloudConflictRef`, that silently disabled sync for the rest of the session.
Because revisions are ordered, the open-time reconcile asks whether the remote
is strictly *ahead* of the cursor rather than merely different, so a remote
that's behind (a restored backup) leaves newer local progress alone.

⚠️ **The web app and the game server both write `save_revision`**, so they ship
together — see [deploy.md](deploy.md#shipping-a-schema-change).

## Updating a running deployment

- **Normal path:** merge to `main`. CI's `verify` + `e2e` gate the automatic deploy
  above. Changing a `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` value requires a redeploy (a re-run), not just an
  env edit — it's inlined at build time.
- **Manual escape hatch (web):** `vercel --prod` from the repo root deploys
  immediately, bypassing the CI gate — for emergencies only.
- **Manual escape hatch (game server):** `bun run deploy:server` (from the repo root —
  it wraps `fly deploy --config server/fly.toml --dockerfile server/Dockerfile`); the
  same command the `deploy-server` job runs. Rooms drain to Postgres on the rollout;
  connected clients reconnect on their back-off ladder and re-sync (they'll see a
  brief "Reconnecting…" badge). **Never run a bare `fly deploy`**: there is no
  Dockerfile at the repo root, so flyctl's framework scanner generates a Next.js
  web-app image (`bun run start`, port 3000) and ships _that_ to the game-server
  app — it crash-loops with exit 127 (`next` needs `node`, absent from the `oven/bun`
  base) and takes online play down until a correct redeploy.
- **Protocol bump (`PROTOCOL_VERSION`):** always the normal path — the number is
  compiled into both sides and a mismatch is a fatal close, so web and game
  server must ship **from the same SHA** (the gated deploy does exactly that;
  never bump one side via an escape hatch). Browsers still on the old bundle
  are refused until a page reload — expected and bounded. Full runbook:
  [protocol.md](protocol.md#version-bump--rollout).
- **Schema change:** land the new migration, then run `bun run db:migrate`
  against production **before** deploying the code that depends on it —
  **unless the migration removes something the old code reads** (a dropped
  column, like `0003`'s `is_anonymous`): then deploy the new code first and
  migrate second, since the old build would error on the missing column while
  the new build just ignores it until the migration lands.

## Troubleshooting

  against production **before** deploying the code that depends on it —
  **unless the migration removes something the old code reads** (a dropped

  - **If the column is written by BOTH the web app and the game server** —

    ship **from the same SHA**, like a protocol bump: the gated deploy does that
    by construction, so take the normal path and never move one side with an
    escape hatch. Half-deployed, the un-updated side keeps writing the blob
    without advancing the revision, so other devices never see the cloud move.
    The migration itself is additive and safe to run first (an old build ignores
    the column), and rolling back the code needs no down-migration.

### Fixed

input.new_string:
### Fixed

- **Renaming a cloud world no longer silently switches off cloud sync on your other devices** (⚠ adds migration `0004`; web + game server must deploy together): `worlds.updatedAt` was doing two unrelated jobs — metadata mtime (what the world list sorts by) and the save revision every device compares to decide whether the cloud moved. Renaming a world bumped it, so every _other_ device's sync cursor went stale over a save that hadn't changed by a single byte. Their next push came back **409 conflict**, and since a conflict latches sync off for the session to avoid clobbering another device, the result was a world that quietly stopped syncing until you noticed. No concurrency needed — one rename did it. The two jobs are now two columns: `updatedAt` stays metadata mtime, while the new monotonic `saveRevision` counts **blob writes and nothing else**, incremented SQL-side by both writers (the browser upload and the game server's room persistence) so concurrent writes can't settle on a stale read. Revision 0 means never saved, which is what lets the server accept a "first upload" without taking the client's word for it. Devices now store revisions (`minecraft_cloud_stamps_v2`), and because revisions are _ordered_ where timestamps were only compared for equality, the open-time reconcile asks whether the cloud is strictly **ahead** of your cursor rather than merely different — so a remote that's behind (a restored backup, a stale replica) can no longer overwrite newer local progress. The migration backfills existing worlds that already hold a blob to revision 1, since 0 would advertise them as never-saved. Also hardens the upload's base check: an unparseable revision is now rejected rather than quietly read as a first upload, which would have handed a stale client a clobber.
- **A malformed save is now refused at the door instead of crashing the engine**:

lines: ### Fixed

+- **Renaming a cloud world no longer silently switches off cloud sync on your other devices** (⚠ adds migration `0004`; web + game server must deploy together): `worlds.updatedAt` was doing two unrelated jobs — metadata mtime (what the world list sorts by) and the save revision every device compares to decide whether the cloud moved. Renaming a world bumped it, so every _other_ device's sync cursor went stale over a save that hadn't changed by a single byte. Their next push came back **409 conflict**, and since a conflict latches sync off for the session to avoid clobbering another device, the result was a world that quietly stopped syncing until you noticed. No concurrency needed — one rename did it. The two jobs are now two columns: `updatedAt` stays metadata mtime, while the new monotonic `saveRevision` counts **blob writes and nothing else**, incremented SQL-side by both writers (the browser upload and the game server's room persistence) so concurrent writes can't settle on a stale read. Revision 0 means never saved, which is what lets the server accept a "first upload" without taking the client's word for it. Devices now store revisions (`minecraft_cloud_stamps_v2`), and because revisions are _ordered_ where timestamps were only compared for equality, the open-time reconcile asks whether the cloud is strictly **ahead** of your cursor rather than merely different — so a remote that's behind (a restored backup, a stale replica) can no longer overwrite newer local progress. The migration backfills existing worlds that already hold a blob to revision 1, since 0 would advertise them as never-saved. Also hardens the upload's base check: an unparseable revision is now rejected rather than quietly read as a first upload, which would have handed a stale client a clobber.

- **A malformed save is now refused at the door instead of crashing the engine**: `parseSave` — the one seam every save reader shares — documented itself as _total_ ("unknown shapes … all yield null") but only checked that the top-level `changes` and `players` were **arrays**, never what was in them. So a current-version save like `{version: 18, seed: 1, changes: [1], players: [null]}` passed validation and then threw deeper in, where nothing is defensive by design: the engine's constructor does `save.players.find((p) => p.id === …)` on the null, and `applySavedChanges` destructures every change as a tuple. It now validates entries — player entries must be objects with a string id, changes must be `[index, blockId]` integer pairs, and a `dimensions` section must carry a usable `changes` array. Malformed **entries drop** (one bad pair must not cost you your world — matching every other reader in the module, which has always dropped rather than thrown), while a malformed **save** still reads as no save. Block ids are bounded to the voxel array's 0–255 storage width, since a larger id wouldn't fail loudly — it would wrap (`300 & 255` = 44) and silently become a _different real block_ — but they're deliberately not allow-listed against `BlockId`, because a hand-maintained ceiling would silently discard legitimate blocks the day someone appends an id and forgets to raise it, trading a cosmetic failure (unknown ids already render magenta) for real data loss. Deep per-field validation stays where it already lives, in the restorers. Separately, the **cloud download** was the one save path that skipped all of this — it cast the decompressed JSON straight to `SaveData`, so a corrupt blob rode into the engine — and now validates like the rest; anything that isn't a save reads as "no save here", which the callers already treat as "keep what's local".

- **An invited player can no longer overwrite a multiplayer world's authoritative save**: `sp-cloud` and `mp` worlds keep their save in the same `worlds.saveBlob` column, but they don't share its ownership — an `sp-cloud` blob **is** the client's upload, while an `mp` blob is the game server's authoritative persistence, which a room reloads as world state on its next boot. `PUT /api/worlds/:id/save` gated on membership but never on `kind`, so anyone holding an invite could upload a crafted `SaveData` over a shared world and have the server adopt it wholesale on the next room boot — inventories, builds, the lot — bypassing the server authority the protocol reserves for itself ("clients cannot invent items or edits", [docs/protocol.md](docs/protocol.md#trust-model)). Nothing legitimate ever uploaded an `mp` world (the in-game push returns early when online, and mp worlds carry no `cloudId`), so uploads are now `sp-cloud`-only — the mirror image of the `mp`-only check the join-ticket path already made. Reads stay membership-gated: a member can already see the world by playing it. Separately, the upload route now rejects an oversized body on its declared `content-length` before buffering it, and stored blobs inflate through a bounded gunzip (gzip runs ~1000:1 on hostile input, so an unbounded inflate turns a few MiB of stored bytes into GiB of heap on a 512 MB VM) — with the kind gate in place a room should only ever read blobs it wrote itself, so that bound is defense in depth rather than a live vector, but it's the seam where stored bytes become engine state and shouldn't trust the row on the far side.

12	   │                   /api/auth/*   better-auth (accounts)
13	   │                   /api/worlds…  world CRUD, invites, cloud saves
14	   │                   /api/worlds/:id/ticket   mints 60s HS256 join ticket
15	   │
16	   └──(ws + ticket)── Game server (Bun, Fly.io)  ── same Postgres
17	                       one authoritative GameEngine room per world (phase 4)
18	```
19	
20	The web app and the game server never talk to each other at runtime: the
21	join ticket (`lib/net/tickets.ts`, signed with the shared
22	`GAME_TICKET_SECRET`) is the only trust link, and both read the same
23	Postgres.
24	
25	## Identity: Local Players and accounts
26	
27	- **Online play is accounts-only** (email/password via better-auth). There is
28	  no anonymous-guest layer: an invite link, cloud sync, or hosting all start
29	  with sign-in/register. Logged-out **Local Players** keep any number of
30	  browser-local profiles and worlds and make **zero** server calls.
31	- **The logged-out root is a welcome gate**
32	  (`components/menu/WelcomeScreen.tsx`): exactly two doors — **Sign in**
33	  (opens the dedicated `AuthScreen`, whose email/password form registers via
34	  its "I need an account" toggle; the form itself is the shared
35	  `AccountForm`) and **Play locally** (the browser-local `ProfileSelect`,
36	  with no account UI on it and a Back to the gate). The gate shows on every
37	  logged-out launch; a signed-in reload skips it — the shell holds a neutral
38	  frame until the session probe answers, then lands on the account home.
39	- When signed in, the menu opens into an **account home**
40	  (`components/menu/AccountProfileSelect.tsx`) listing that account's
41	  server-side profiles (create/rename/delete, capped at `MAX_ONLINE_PROFILES`,
42	  synced across devices); picking one shows its worlds (`OnlineWorldSelect`)
43	  in two sections: **Online Worlds** (server-hosted mp rooms; the join ticket
44	  carries the profile's name/skin) and **Singleplayer** (`sp-cloud` worlds —
45	  full client-side engine, **no game server**, saves synced to the account so
46	  any signed-in device continues them). Owned worlds of both kinds share the
47	  `MAX_WORLDS_PER_PROFILE` cap. Worlds joined by invite are account-level
48	  memberships, so they appear under **every** profile with a "Joined" tag;
49	  so do singleplayer saves uploaded from the local menus (`profileId` null —
50	  account-level).
51	- Local worlds are **hidden but preserved** while signed in — never deleted,
52	  never auto-uploaded. The account home's quiet **"Local worlds on this
53	  browser"** footer link opens the local menus without signing out (that's
54	  also where cloud-save sync lives); "Back to account" returns. Signing out
55	  lands on the welcome gate.
56	- Sessions are better-auth cookies; the game server never sees them.
57	- The compact Account panel (`components/menu/AccountPanel.tsx` — logged out
58	  it offers **Sign in** and **Create account** side by side, expanding into
59	  the shared `AccountForm`) now serves **only** the `/join/<token>` invite
60	  landing page; the main menu routes through the welcome gate instead.
61	
62	## Worlds, invites, cloud saves
63	
64	`lib/online/worldsService.ts` owns the rules (membership-gated reads that
65	present as `not-found` so ids can't be probed; owner-gated rename/delete/
66	invite; idempotent invite acceptance with expiry/max-uses). The `app/api`
67	routes are thin HTTP adapters over it.
68	
69	Single-player cloud saves are gzipped `SaveData` blobs (`lib/game/
70	cloudSaves.ts` — block diffs compress extremely well) with last-write-wins
71	concurrency: each device sends the `saveRevision` it last saw
72	(`x-base-revision`); a mismatch is **409** and the pushing client stops
73	syncing and warns (rather than clobber the other device), then adopts the
74	newer save on the next open.
75	
76	**Two clocks, deliberately.** `worlds.updatedAt` is metadata mtime — "last
77	touched", what the world list orders by. `worlds.saveRevision` counts **blob
78	writes and nothing else**: it is the sync cursor devices compare (stored per
79	world under `minecraft_cloud_stamps_v2`) and the CAS token their uploads race
80	on, incremented SQL-side by both writers (`putSaveBlob` and the game server's

82	Revision `0` means never saved, which is what makes "first upload" checkable
83	without trusting the client. They must stay separate: while `updatedAt` served

87	Because revisions are ordered, the open-time reconcile asks whether the remote

89	that's behind (a restored backup) leaves newer local progress alone.
90

92	from the same SHA — see [deploy.md](deploy.md#updating-a-running-deployment).
93

feat(db): add worlds.saveRevision as the save cursor

worlds.updatedAt was doing two unrelated jobs: metadata mtime (what the
world list orders by) and the save revision every device compares to
decide whether the cloud moved.

So renaming a world bumped it, and every OTHER device's sync cursor went
stale over a save that had not changed by a byte. Their next push came
back 409, and since a conflict latches cloudConflictRef to avoid
clobbering another device, cloud sync silently switched off for the rest
of the session. No concurrency required — one rename did it. A read of
the row had the same shape of problem waiting.

Two jobs, two columns. updatedAt stays metadata mtime; saveRevision
counts blob writes and nothing else. Revision 0 means never saved, which
is what lets putSaveBlob accept a "first upload" without taking the
client's word for it. Both writers — the browser upload and the game
server's room persistence — increment it SQL-side, so concurrent writes
can't settle on a value read earlier.

Revisions are ordered where timestamps were only compared for equality,
so the open-time reconcile now asks whether the remote is strictly AHEAD
of the cursor rather than merely different: a remote that is behind (a
restored backup, a stale replica) no longer overwrites newer local
progress.

This lands as one commit because it cannot be split: the schema, both
writers and the client's cursor have to move together or cloud sync
breaks at the intermediate commit.

Details worth knowing:

- The migration's backfill is load-bearing, and is the one hand-written
  line in it (the ALTER is generated). Existing worlds that already hold
  a blob start at revision 1 — leaving them at 0 would advertise them as
  never-saved and invite a cursor-less client to clobber them.
- Client stamps move to minecraft_cloud_stamps_v2 rather than migrating:
  a leftover ISO timestamp compared against a revision would read as
  "the cloud moved" forever. Starting empty costs nothing, because the
  open-time pull sets a cursor before anything pushes.
- The headers are renamed (x-save-revision / x-base-revision) since
  their meaning changed. Note x-save-version is the save FORMAT version
  — a different thing with an adjacent name.
- An unparseable base revision is rejected rather than quietly read as a
  first upload, which would hand a stale client a clobber.

Adds db/migrations.test.ts: every other suite builds its schema from
db/ddl.ts, so a broken migration would stay green across the whole suite
and fail only in production. It applies the committed migrations in
order onto an empty PGlite and pins 0004's backfill.

Deploy: additive migration, safe to run first, no down-migration needed
to roll the code back. But web and game server both write the column, so
they must ship from the same SHA — half-deployed, the un-updated side
writes blobs without advancing the revision and other devices never see
the cloud move. Runbook updated in docs/deploy.md.
EOF

content.text:
**Commit 4 is in (`720616d`)** — the headline fix. Full gate green: 1520 pass, build, format, typecheck, lint all clean.

The rename bug is now covered by a test that would have failed before: the old guard was `eq(updatedAt, baseUpdatedAt)`, and `renameWorld` set `updatedAt = now()`, so a post-rename push matched zero rows and returned `conflict`. That test now demands `ok: true`.

Three things worth flagging from this one:

**The generated migration was wrong on its own.** `drizzle-kit` produced `ADD COLUMN save_revision integer DEFAULT 0 NOT NULL` — which would mark *every existing world* as never-saved, and revision 0 is precisely what lets a cursor-less client claim a first upload and clobber a real save. The backfill (`UPDATE ... WHERE save_blob IS NOT NULL`) is the one hand-written line, so it's the one that can be wrong.

**Which is why I added `db/migrations.test.ts`.** Every other suite builds its schema from the hand-maintained `db/ddl.ts`, *not* from the migrations — so a broken migration passes the entire test suite and fails only in production. That gap seems worth closing permanently, not just for this migration.

**I also tightened one thing beyond the plan.** Revisions are *ordered*, where the old timestamp cursor was only compared with `===`. So the reconcile now asks whether the remote is strictly *ahead* rather than merely different — a remote that's *behind* your cursor (a restored backup, a stale replica) no longer overwrites newer local progress. The old code would have adopted it.

Deploy note carried into `docs/deploy.md`: the migration is additive and safe to run first, and rolling back the code needs no down-migration — but web and game server both write the column, so they must ship from the same SHA. Half-deployed, the stale side writes blobs without advancing the revision and no device ever sees the cloud move.

Next: commit 5, serializing the cloud pushes — the other half of this bug, where a phone backgrounding fires `pagehide` and `visibilitychange` and conflicts with itself.

Each fired its own upload immediately, so two pushes went out carrying the same base revision; the server accepted one and 409'd the other, and a 409 latches syncing off for the session to avoid clobbering another device. The result: a single device switched off its own cloud sync by conflicting with **itself**, and the toast blamed a device that didn't exist. Uploads now go through a latest-wins queue — one in flight, the newest snapshot behind it, superseded snapshots dropped (they describe the same world). The snapshot is taken when a push is _requested_ rather than when it runs, so the unload flush still uploads the state as of the unload. Separately, the open-time reconcile advanced this device's sync cursor _before_ the downloaded save was stored locally: if that write failed, the device claimed a save it didn't have and every later open read the cloud as "not ahead" and declined to adopt it — stranding the cloud save on that device permanently. The cursor now moves only once the local write has durably committed.
- **Renaming a cloud world no longer silently switches off cloud sync on your other devices**

lines: ### Fixed

+- **Backgrounding the game on a phone no longer switches off its own cloud sync**: six places push a cloud-linked world's save (autosave, three unload listeners, hardcore game-over, unmount, manual save) and several fire at once — backgrounding a mobile tab raises **both** `visibilitychange` and `pagehide`. Each fired its own upload immediately, so two pushes went out carrying the same base revision; the server accepted one and 409'd the other, and a 409 latches syncing off for the session to avoid clobbering another device. The result: a single device switched off its own cloud sync by conflicting with **itself**, and the toast blamed a device that didn't exist. Uploads now go through a latest-wins queue — one in flight, the newest snapshot behind it, superseded snapshots dropped (they describe the same world). The snapshot is taken when a push is _requested_ rather than when it runs, so the unload flush still uploads the state as of the unload. Separately, the open-time reconcile advanced this device's sync cursor _before_ the downloaded save was stored locally: if that write failed, the device claimed a save it didn't have and every later open read the cloud as "not ahead" and declined to adopt it — stranding the cloud save on that device permanently. The cursor now moves only once the local write has durably committed.

- **Renaming a cloud world no longer silently switches off cloud sync on your other devices** (⚠ adds migration `0004`; web + game server must deploy together): `worlds.updatedAt` was doing two unrelated jobs — metadata mtime (what the world list sorts by) and the save revision every device compares to decide whether the cloud moved. Renaming a world bumped it, so every _other_ device's sync cursor went stale over a save that hadn't changed by a single byte. Their next push came back **409 conflict**, and since a conflict latches sync off for the session to avoid clobbering another device, the result was a world that quietly stopped syncing until you noticed. No concurrency needed — one rename did it. The two jobs are now two columns: `updatedAt` stays metadata mtime, while the new monotonic `saveRevision` counts **blob writes and nothing else**, incremented SQL-side by both writers (the browser upload and the game server's room persistence) so concurrent writes can't settle on a stale read. Revision 0 means never saved, which is what lets the server accept a "first upload" without taking the client's word for it. Devices now store revisions (`minecraft_cloud_stamps_v2`), and because revisions are _ordered_ where timestamps were only compared for equality, the open-time reconcile asks whether the cloud is strictly **ahead** of your cursor rather than merely different — so a remote that's behind (a restored backup, a stale replica) can no longer overwrite newer local progress. The migration backfills existing worlds that already hold a blob to revision 1, since 0 would advertise them as never-saved. Also hardens the upload's base check: an unparseable revision is now rejected rather than quietly read as a first upload, which would have handed a stale client a clobber.

- **A malformed save is now refused at the door instead of crashing the engine**: `parseSave` — the one seam every save reader shares — documented itself as _total_ ("unknown shapes … all yield null") but only checked that the top-level `changes` and `players` were **arrays**, never what was in them. So a current-version save like `{version: 18, seed: 1, changes: [1], players: [null]}` passed validation and then threw deeper in, where nothing is defensive by design: the engine's constructor does `save.players.find((p) => p.id === …)` on the null, and `applySavedChanges` destructures every change as a tuple. It now validates entries — player entries must be objects with a string id, changes must be `[index, blockId]` integer pairs, and a `dimensions` section must carry a usable `changes` array. Malformed **entries drop** (one bad pair must not cost you your world — matching every other reader in the module, which has always dropped rather than thrown), while a malformed **save** still reads as no save. Block ids are bounded to the voxel array's 0–255 storage width, since a larger id wouldn't fail loudly — it would wrap (`300 & 255` = 44) and silently become a _different real block_ — but they're deliberately not allow-listed against `BlockId`, because a hand-maintained ceiling would silently discard legitimate blocks the day someone appends an id and forgets to raise it, trading a cosmetic failure (unknown ids already render magenta) for real data loss. Deep per-field validation stays where it already lives, in the restorers. Separately, the **cloud download** was the one save path that skipped all of this — it cast the decompressed JSON straight to `SaveData`, so a corrupt blob rode into the engine — and now validates like the rest; anything that isn't a save reads as "no save here", which the callers already treat as "keep what's local".

1	# Online: accounts, cloud saves, multiplayer
2	
3	How the online stack fits together, and how to run it. The offline
4	single-player game needs **none** of this: without an online action, the
5	client never makes an auth request (the `minecraft_online_v1` localStorage
6	flag gates even the session check).
7	
8	## The pieces
9	
10	```
11	Browser ──(cookies)── Next.js app          ── Neon/Postgres
12	   │                   /api/auth/*   better-auth (accounts)
13	   │                   /api/worlds…  world CRUD, invites, cloud saves
14	   │                   /api/worlds/:id/ticket   mints 60s HS256 join ticket
15	   │
16	   └──(ws + ticket)── Game server (Bun, Fly.io)  ── same Postgres
17	                       one authoritative GameEngine room per world (phase 4)
18	```
19	
20	The web app and the game server never talk to each other at runtime: the
21	join ticket (`lib/net/tickets.ts`, signed with the shared
22	`GAME_TICKET_SECRET`) is the only trust link, and both read the same
23	Postgres.
24	
25	## Identity: Local Players and accounts
26	
27	- **Online play is accounts-only** (email/password via better-auth). There is
28	  no anonymous-guest layer: an invite link, cloud sync, or hosting all start
29	  with sign-in/register. Logged-out **Local Players** keep any number of
30	  browser-local profiles and worlds and make **zero** server calls.
31	- **The logged-out root is a welcome gate**
32	  (`components/menu/WelcomeScreen.tsx`): exactly two doors — **Sign in**
33	  (opens the dedicated `AuthScreen`, whose email/password form registers via
34	  its "I need an account" toggle; the form itself is the shared
35	  `AccountForm`) and **Play locally** (the browser-local `ProfileSelect`,
36	  with no account UI on it and a Back to the gate). The gate shows on every
37	  logged-out launch; a signed-in reload skips it — the shell holds a neutral
38	  frame until the session probe answers, then lands on the account home.
39	- When signed in, the menu opens into an **account home**
40	  (`components/menu/AccountProfileSelect.tsx`) listing that account's
41	  server-side profiles (create/rename/delete, capped at `MAX_ONLINE_PROFILES`,
42	  synced across devices); picking one shows its worlds (`OnlineWorldSelect`)
43	  in two sections: **Online Worlds** (server-hosted mp rooms; the join ticket
44	  carries the profile's name/skin) and **Singleplayer** (`sp-cloud` worlds —
45	  full client-side engine, **no game server**, saves synced to the account so
46	  any signed-in device continues them). Owned worlds of both kinds share the
47	  `MAX_WORLDS_PER_PROFILE` cap. Worlds joined by invite are account-level
48	  memberships, so they appear under **every** profile with a "Joined" tag;
49	  so do singleplayer saves uploaded from the local menus (`profileId` null —
50	  account-level).
51	- Local worlds are **hidden but preserved** while signed in — never deleted,
52	  never auto-uploaded. The account home's quiet **"Local worlds on this
53	  browser"** footer link opens the local menus without signing out (that's
54	  also where cloud-save sync lives); "Back to account" returns. Signing out
55	  lands on the welcome gate.
56	- Sessions are better-auth cookies; the game server never sees them.
57	- The compact Account panel (`components/menu/AccountPanel.tsx` — logged out
58	  it offers **Sign in** and **Create account** side by side, expanding into
59	  the shared `AccountForm`) now serves **only** the `/join/<token>` invite
60	  landing page; the main menu routes through the welcome gate instead.
61	
62	## Worlds, invites, cloud saves
63	
64	`lib/online/worldsService.ts` owns the rules (membership-gated reads that
65	present as `not-found` so ids can't be probed; owner-gated rename/delete/
66	invite; idempotent invite acceptance with expiry/max-uses). The `app/api`
67	routes are thin HTTP adapters over it.
68	
69	Single-player cloud saves are gzipped `SaveData` blobs (`lib/game/
70	cloudSaves.ts` — block diffs compress extremely well) with last-write-wins
71	concurrency: each device sends the `saveRevision` it last saw
72	(`x-base-revision`); a mismatch is **409** and the pushing client stops
73	syncing and warns (rather than clobber the other device), then adopts the
74	newer save on the next open.
75	
76	**Two clocks, deliberately.** `worlds.updatedAt` is metadata mtime — "last
77	touched", what the world list orders by. `worlds.saveRevision` counts **blob
78	writes and nothing else**: it is the sync cursor devices compare (stored per

fix(game): serialize cloud pushes and make the sync cursor durable

Two ways a single device sabotaged its own cloud sync.

Self-inflicted conflicts. Six call sites push a cloud-linked world's
save — autosave, the three unload listeners, hardcore game-over, unmount,
manual save — and several fire together: backgrounding a phone raises
visibilitychange AND pagehide. Each fired its own upload immediately, so
two pushes went out carrying the same base revision. The server took one
and 409'd the other, and a 409 latches syncing off for the session (it
means "another device won, don't clobber them"). So one device switched
off its own sync by conflicting with itself, and the toast blamed a
device that did not exist.

Uploads now go through a latest-wins queue: one in flight, the newest
snapshot behind it, superseded snapshots dropped — they describe the same
world, so only the newest is worth sending. The snapshot is serialized
when a push is REQUESTED rather than when it runs, so the unload flush
still uploads the state as of the unload.

Worth noting the queue makes the unload path strictly better, not worse.
Previously a flush racing an in-flight autosave fired a second fetch
that might land; now it may be dropped if the page dies first. But that
race is exactly the bug: the old second fetch 409'd, latched the
conflict, AND still didn't persist the newer state. Now the in-flight
push lands, the cloud is at most one autosave behind, the local
IndexedDB save is unaffected, and the next open reconciles.

Cursor durability. The open-time reconcile advanced this device's cursor
before the caller stored the downloaded save. If that write failed, the
device claimed a revision it did not hold — and since the reconcile only
adopts a remote strictly AHEAD of the cursor, every later open then read
the cloud as "not ahead" and declined to adopt, stranding the cloud save
on that device permanently. commitCursor() is now the caller's to call
once the local write has durably committed.

The queue lives in its own module rather than inline in the hook:
useMinecraftGame has no tests (it wires engine+renderer+audio+input, so a
harness is a project of its own), and shipping untested concurrency logic
into it is how this class of bug got here. As a standalone factory it
needs no React and is driven in tests by a hand-resolved push, so overlap
is deterministic rather than timed.

Same shape as the save store's per-world write queue, deliberately not
shared with it: different resource, different failure mode (a 409 latch
rather than a retry), and saveStore's loop is entangled with IndexedDB
tombstones and its localStorage fallback.
EOF

lines: ### Fixed

+- **A crashed game server no longer loses a session's progress that involved no block edit**: an online room persisted on its 60s interval only when a "dirty" flag was set — and exactly five things set it: dimension travel, a nether-shard evict, join, leave, and block-edit events. Everything else a live session does — inventory, health, hunger, status effects, XP, statistics, advancements, mob and container state, position — marked nothing. Mine nothing for twenty minutes while fighting, trading, brewing and levelling, and a hard crash (SIGKILL, an OOM, a Fly host fault) rolled all of it back; graceful paths were fine, since join/leave mark dirty and shutdown always persists, so this only ever showed up as a crash losing more than it should. An **occupied** room now persists on the interval regardless of the flag, which stays on only to decide whether an empty room still owes a write — chasing every mutation site would be a list to keep in sync forever, and one omission is a silent loss. Persistence also **coalesces**: it was fire-and-forget with no in-flight guard, so two stores could overlap on an unguarded `UPDATE` and land out of order, the older winning; and a store's completion could clear the dirty flag against an edit that arrived _during_ the write, swallowing it until the next unrelated block edit. Now one store runs at a time with at most one follow-up queued, the flag is cleared against the snapshot actually taken, and a failed write re-marks the room dirty to retry rather than dropping the state.

- **Backgrounding the game on a phone no longer switches off its own cloud sync**: six places push a cloud-linked world's save (autosave, three unload listeners, hardcore game-over, unmount, manual save) and several fire at once — backgrounding a mobile tab raises **both** `visibilitychange` and `pagehide`. Each fired its own upload immediately, so two pushes went out carrying the same base revision; the server accepted one and 409'd the other, and a 409 latches syncing off for the session to avoid clobbering another device. The result: a single device switched off its own cloud sync by conflicting with **itself**, and the toast blamed a device that didn't exist. Uploads now go through a latest-wins queue — one in flight, the newest snapshot behind it, superseded snapshots dropped (they describe the same world). The snapshot is taken when a push is _requested_ rather than when it runs, so the unload flush still uploads the state as of the unload. Separately, the open-time reconcile advanced this device's sync cursor _before_ the downloaded save was stored locally: if that write failed, the device claimed a save it didn't have and every later open read the cloud as "not ahead" and declined to adopt it — stranding the cloud save on that device permanently. The cursor now moves only once the local write has durably committed.

- **Renaming a cloud world no longer silently switches off cloud sync on your other devices** (⚠ adds migration `0004`; web + game server must deploy together): `worlds.updatedAt` was doing two unrelated jobs — metadata mtime (what the world list sorts by) and the save revision every device compares to decide whether the cloud moved. Renaming a world bumped it, so every _other_ device's sync cursor went stale over a save that hadn't changed by a single byte. Their next push came back **409 conflict**, and since a conflict latches sync off for the session to avoid clobbering another device, the result was a world that quietly stopped syncing until you noticed. No concurrency needed — one rename did it. The two jobs are now two columns: `updatedAt` stays metadata mtime, while the new monotonic `saveRevision` counts **blob writes and nothing else**, incremented SQL-side by both writers (the browser upload and the game server's room persistence) so concurrent writes can't settle on a stale read. Revision 0 means never saved, which is what lets the server accept a "first upload" without taking the client's word for it. Devices now store revisions (`minecraft_cloud_stamps_v2`), and because revisions are _ordered_ where timestamps were only compared for equality, the open-time reconcile asks whether the cloud is strictly **ahead** of your cursor rather than merely different — so a remote that's behind (a restored backup, a stale replica) can no longer overwrite newer local progress. The migration backfills existing worlds that already hold a blob to revision 1, since 0 would advertise them as never-saved. Also hardens the upload's base check: an unparseable revision is now rejected rather than quietly read as a first upload, which would have handed a stale client a clobber.

- **A malformed save is now refused at the door instead of crashing the engine**: `parseSave` — the one seam every save reader shares — documented itself as _total_ ("unknown shapes … all yield null") but only checked that the top-level `changes` and `players` were **arrays**, never what was in them. So a current-version save like `{version: 18, seed: 1, changes: [1], players: [null]}` passed validation and then threw deeper in, where nothing is defensive by design: the engine's constructor does `save.players.find((p) => p.id === …)` on the null, and `applySavedChanges` destructures every change as a tuple. It now validates entries — player entries must be objects with a string id, changes must be `[index, blockId]` integer pairs, and a `dimensions` section must carry a usable `changes` array. Malformed **entries drop** (one bad pair must not cost you your world — matching every other reader in the module, which has always dropped rather than thrown), while a malformed **save** still reads as no save. Block ids are bounded to the voxel array's 0–255 storage width, since a larger id wouldn't fail loudly — it would wrap (`300 & 255` = 44) and silently become a _different real block_ — but they're deliberately not allow-listed against `BlockId`, because a hand-maintained ceiling would silently discard legitimate blocks the day someone appends an id and forgets to raise it, trading a cosmetic failure (unknown ids already render magenta) for real data loss. Deep per-field validation stays where it already lives, in the restorers. Separately, the **cloud download** was the one save path that skipped all of this — it cast the decompressed JSON straight to `SaveData`, so a corrupt blob rode into the engine — and now validates like the rest; anything that isn't a save reads as "no save here", which the callers already treat as "keep what's local".

fix(server): persist active rooms reliably

A room persisted on its 60s interval only when a dirty flag was set, and
exactly five things set it: dimension travel, a nether-shard evict, join,
leave, and block-edit events.

Everything else a live session does marked nothing — inventory, health,
hunger, effects, XP, statistics, advancements, mob and container state,
position. So twenty minutes of fighting, trading, brewing and levelling
without mining a single block left the room "clean", and a hard crash
rolled all of it back. Graceful paths hid it: join/leave mark dirty and
shutdown always persists, so this only ever surfaced as a crash losing
more than it should.

An occupied room now persists on the interval whatever the flag says. The
flag stays, demoted to answering one question: does an EMPTY room still
owe a write (block edits, then everyone left). Chasing every mutation
site was the alternative — a list to keep in sync forever, where one
omission is a silent data loss, which is exactly how this got here.

Stores also coalesce. persist() was fire-and-forget with no in-flight
guard, and storeWorld has no version guard, so two overlapping stores
raced: last write wins, and out of order the OLDER snapshot could be the
one that lands. Composing + gzipping a whole world is expensive enough
that overlap is not hypothetical under load. Now one store runs at a
time with at most one follow-up queued (a third would compose the same
state), and shutdown()'s await therefore always resolves on a store that
saw the final state rather than racing an interval store already in
flight.

Two smaller correctness fixes in the same seam:

- The flag is cleared against the snapshot just composed, not against
  whatever is true when the write returns. A mutation landing DURING a
  write used to be swallowed by that write's success, invisible until
  some later block edit happened to re-mark the room.
- A failed store re-marks the room dirty instead of leaving it clean and
  dropping the state.

Verified the interval test fails against the old dirty-flag-only trigger.
EOF

lines: ### Fixed

+- **Rejoining a world just as it's evicted can no longer resurrect it from stale state**: an idle room was dropped from the registry _before_ its shutdown finished persisting, and that final write is a whole-world gzip plus a Postgres round-trip — a window wide enough to land in. A join arriving inside it found no room, took the load path, and read the blob the shutdown was still in the middle of replacing. The process then held **two** `Room` objects for one world, both writing the same row through an `UPDATE` with no version guard: last write wins, and the eviction's is typically the older one, so the evicted room's final state — the last minutes before it emptied — silently lost. Eviction now hands the room from "live" to "closing" in one step: it leaves the registry (nobody may join a room that's closing its sockets) and a load for that world waits for the shutdown's write to land before reading the row, so it can only ever build a room from post-shutdown state.

- **A crashed game server no longer loses a session's progress that involved no block edit**: an online room persisted on its 60s interval only when a "dirty" flag was set — and exactly five things set it: dimension travel, a nether-shard evict, join, leave, and block-edit events. Everything else a live session does — inventory, health, hunger, status effects, XP, statistics, advancements, mob and container state, position — marked nothing. Mine nothing for twenty minutes while fighting, trading, brewing and levelling, and a hard crash (SIGKILL, an OOM, a Fly host fault) rolled all of it back; graceful paths were fine, since join/leave mark dirty and shutdown always persists, so this only ever showed up as a crash losing more than it should. An **occupied** room now persists on the interval regardless of the flag, which stays on only to decide whether an empty room still owes a write — chasing every mutation site would be a list to keep in sync forever, and one omission is a silent loss. Persistence also **coalesces**: it was fire-and-forget with no in-flight guard, so two stores could overlap on an unguarded `UPDATE` and land out of order, the older winning; and a store's completion could clear the dirty flag against an edit that arrived _during_ the write, swallowing it until the next unrelated block edit. Now one store runs at a time with at most one follow-up queued, the flag is cleared against the snapshot actually taken, and a failed write re-marks the room dirty to retry rather than dropping the state.

- **Backgrounding the game on a phone no longer switches off its own cloud sync**: six places push a cloud-linked world's save (autosave, three unload listeners, hardcore game-over, unmount, manual save) and several fire at once — backgrounding a mobile tab raises **both** `visibilitychange` and `pagehide`. Each fired its own upload immediately, so two pushes went out carrying the same base revision; the server accepted one and 409'd the other, and a 409 latches syncing off for the session to avoid clobbering another device. The result: a single device switched off its own cloud sync by conflicting with **itself**, and the toast blamed a device that didn't exist. Uploads now go through a latest-wins queue — one in flight, the newest snapshot behind it, superseded snapshots dropped (they describe the same world). The snapshot is taken when a push is _requested_ rather than when it runs, so the unload flush still uploads the state as of the unload. Separately, the open-time reconcile advanced this device's sync cursor _before_ the downloaded save was stored locally: if that write failed, the device claimed a save it didn't have and every later open read the cloud as "not ahead" and declined to adopt it — stranding the cloud save on that device permanently. The cursor now moves only once the local write has durably committed.

- **Renaming a cloud world no longer silently switches off cloud sync on your other devices** (⚠ adds migration `0004`; web + game server must deploy together): `worlds.updatedAt` was doing two unrelated jobs — metadata mtime (what the world list sorts by) and the save revision every device compares to decide whether the cloud moved. Renaming a world bumped it, so every _other_ device's sync cursor went stale over a save that hadn't changed by a single byte. Their next push came back **409 conflict**, and since a conflict latches sync off for the session to avoid clobbering another device, the result was a world that quietly stopped syncing until you noticed. No concurrency needed — one rename did it. The two jobs are now two columns: `updatedAt` stays metadata mtime, while the new monotonic `saveRevision` counts **blob writes and nothing else**, incremented SQL-side by both writers (the browser upload and the game server's room persistence) so concurrent writes can't settle on a stale read. Revision 0 means never saved, which is what lets the server accept a "first upload" without taking the client's word for it. Devices now store revisions (`minecraft_cloud_stamps_v2`), and because revisions are _ordered_ where timestamps were only compared for equality, the open-time reconcile asks whether the cloud is strictly **ahead** of your cursor rather than merely different — so a remote that's behind (a restored backup, a stale replica) can no longer overwrite newer local progress. The migration backfills existing worlds that already hold a blob to revision 1, since 0 would advertise them as never-saved. Also hardens the upload's base check: an unparseable revision is now rejected rather than quietly read as a first upload, which would have handed a stale client a clobber.

bun run format >/dev/null 2>&1; bun run lint 2>&1 | tail -2; bun run typecheck 2>&1 | tail -1; git add -A && git commit -q -F- <<'EOF'
fix(net): process inbound frames in order

processServerFrame is async, and onServerFrame fired frames at it
without waiting. The binary worldSync awaits gunzip — several macrotasks
in a browser (DecompressionStream via a Response) — so a text `tick`
arriving during that await ran to completion first, applied its blocks,
and then the older worldSync landed on top and clobbered them.

The delayLine comment three functions up already asserts the FIFO this
depends on ("the seq/journal handling downstream assumes order"), but it
only ordered when frames START processing, not when their async work
COMPLETES. So the invariant the code claimed was not actually upheld.

Frames now chain through a one-at-a-time inbound queue: each frame's
promise runs after the previous one settles, so completion order matches
arrival. Errors are swallowed per frame so one bad frame can't wedge the
chain.

Server-side this is reachable: room.ts sends the join worldSync after
registering the client, so the tick loop can emit a tick to that
connection before the worldSync is on the wire — the exact
binary-then-text overlap.

The regression test emits a gzipped worldSync and a tick targeting the
same cell back-to-back with no await between, and asserts the later
frame wins. It fails against the old concurrent dispatch even under Bun,
whose gunzip is "synchronous" but still yields once — enough for the
text frame to slip ahead. Also corrected the delayLine comment to say
which layer orders what.
EOF
git log --oneline -1

lines: ### Fixed

+- **A brief network blip in an online world reconnects cleanly instead of sometimes killing the session**: the client's socket-close handling wasn't idempotent. A browser fires **both** `error` and `close` for an abnormal drop, and both ran the same close path — so one blip scheduled two reconnects, burned two rungs of the back-off ladder, minted two tickets, and raced two handshakes. The second handshake's join then kicked the first connection (`CLOSE_KICKED`, a fatal code), and because that orphaned socket's handlers were still bound, its close drove the session that had _just reconnected_ straight to "disconnected". A transient blip could therefore take down a session that had already recovered. Each socket now carries a connection generation: a close is acted on only for the live generation (a superseded socket's late close is ignored), and acting on one advances the generation so the same socket's error+close pair schedules exactly one reconnect. The reconnect timer is also single — a new rung clears any pending one rather than orphaning it. (Networking-only; no protocol or save change.)

- **Rejoining a world just as it's evicted can no longer resurrect it from stale state**: an idle room was dropped from the registry _before_ its shutdown finished persisting, and that final write is a whole-world gzip plus a Postgres round-trip — a window wide enough to land in. A join arriving inside it found no room, took the load path, and read the blob the shutdown was still in the middle of replacing. The process then held **two** `Room` objects for one world, both writing the same row through an `UPDATE` with no version guard: last write wins, and the eviction's is typically the older one, so the evicted room's final state — the last minutes before it emptied — silently lost. Eviction now hands the room from "live" to "closing" in one step: it leaves the registry (nobody may join a room that's closing its sockets) and a load for that world waits for the shutdown's write to land before reading the row, so it can only ever build a room from post-shutdown state.

- **A crashed game server no longer loses a session's progress that involved no block edit**: an online room persisted on its 60s interval only when a "dirty" flag was set — and exactly five things set it: dimension travel, a nether-shard evict, join, leave, and block-edit events. Everything else a live session does — inventory, health, hunger, status effects, XP, statistics, advancements, mob and container state, position — marked nothing. Mine nothing for twenty minutes while fighting, trading, brewing and levelling, and a hard crash (SIGKILL, an OOM, a Fly host fault) rolled all of it back; graceful paths were fine, since join/leave mark dirty and shutdown always persists, so this only ever showed up as a crash losing more than it should. An **occupied** room now persists on the interval regardless of the flag, which stays on only to decide whether an empty room still owes a write — chasing every mutation site would be a list to keep in sync forever, and one omission is a silent loss. Persistence also **coalesces**: it was fire-and-forget with no in-flight guard, so two stores could overlap on an unguarded `UPDATE` and land out of order, the older winning; and a store's completion could clear the dirty flag against an edit that arrived _during_ the write, swallowing it until the next unrelated block edit. Now one store runs at a time with at most one follow-up queued, the flag is cleared against the snapshot actually taken, and a failed write re-marks the room dirty to retry rather than dropping the state.

- **Backgrounding the game on a phone no longer switches off its own cloud sync**: six places push a cloud-linked world's save (autosave, three unload listeners, hardcore game-over, unmount, manual save) and several fire at once — backgrounding a mobile tab raises **both** `visibilitychange` and `pagehide`. Each fired its own upload immediately, so two pushes went out carrying the same base revision; the server accepted one and 409'd the other, and a 409 latches syncing off for the session to avoid clobbering another device. The result: a single device switched off its own cloud sync by conflicting with **itself**, and the toast blamed a device that didn't exist. Uploads now go through a latest-wins queue — one in flight, the newest snapshot behind it, superseded snapshots dropped (they describe the same world). The snapshot is taken when a push is _requested_ rather than when it runs, so the unload flush still uploads the state as of the unload. Separately, the open-time reconcile advanced this device's sync cursor _before_ the downloaded save was stored locally: if that write failed, the device claimed a save it didn't have and every later open read the cloud as "not ahead" and declined to adopt it — stranding the cloud save on that device permanently. The cursor now moves only once the local write has durably committed.

lines: ### Fixed

+- **`POST /api/worlds` validates its body instead of trusting it**: the create-world handler cast the request JSON straight to its input type and passed it on, and the service checked only the name, kind, and that the seed was finite. So a hand-rolled request could set `worldType`/`gameMode`/`difficulty` to anything — the columns have no DB-level enum and the game server casts them straight into the engine at room boot — send a seed past int4 (a Postgres overflow surfaced as a 500, not a clean rejection), or set a non-string name that threw on `.trim()`. It now validates each field through the same `isWorldType`/`isGameMode`/`isDifficulty` guards the client already uses, bounds the seed to the column's range, and type-checks the rest. It also closes a **quota bypass**: `MAX_WORLDS_PER_PROFILE` was only checked when a `profileId` was supplied, so omitting it created uncapped, profile-less worlds — `mp` worlds (always profile-scoped in the UI) now require one, while `sp-cloud` stays account-level for the upload path. Nothing legitimate changes; the real client always sent valid values.

- **A brief network blip in an online world reconnects cleanly instead of sometimes killing the session**: the client's socket-close handling wasn't idempotent. A browser fires **both** `error` and `close` for an abnormal drop, and both ran the same close path — so one blip scheduled two reconnects, burned two rungs of the back-off ladder, minted two tickets, and raced two handshakes. The second handshake's join then kicked the first connection (`CLOSE_KICKED`, a fatal code), and because that orphaned socket's handlers were still bound, its close drove the session that had _just reconnected_ straight to "disconnected". A transient blip could therefore take down a session that had already recovered. Each socket now carries a connection generation: a close is acted on only for the live generation (a superseded socket's late close is ignored), and acting on one advances the generation so the same socket's error+close pair schedules exactly one reconnect. The reconnect timer is also single — a new rung clears any pending one rather than orphaning it. (Networking-only; no protocol or save change.)

- **Rejoining a world just as it's evicted can no longer resurrect it from stale state**: an idle room was dropped from the registry _before_ its shutdown finished persisting, and that final write is a whole-world gzip plus a Postgres round-trip — a window wide enough to land in. A join arriving inside it found no room, took the load path, and read the blob the shutdown was still in the middle of replacing. The process then held **two** `Room` objects for one world, both writing the same row through an `UPDATE` with no version guard: last write wins, and the eviction's is typically the older one, so the evicted room's final state — the last minutes before it emptied — silently lost. Eviction now hands the room from "live" to "closing" in one step: it leaves the registry (nobody may join a room that's closing its sockets) and a load for that world waits for the shutdown's write to land before reading the row, so it can only ever build a room from post-shutdown state.

- **A crashed game server no longer loses a session's progress that involved no block edit**: an online room persisted on its 60s interval only when a "dirty" flag was set — and exactly five things set it: dimension travel, a nether-shard evict, join, leave, and block-edit events. Everything else a live session does — inventory, health, hunger, status effects, XP, statistics, advancements, mob and container state, position — marked nothing. Mine nothing for twenty minutes while fighting, trading, brewing and levelling, and a hard crash (SIGKILL, an OOM, a Fly host fault) rolled all of it back; graceful paths were fine, since join/leave mark dirty and shutdown always persists, so this only ever showed up as a crash losing more than it should. An **occupied** room now persists on the interval regardless of the flag, which stays on only to decide whether an empty room still owes a write — chasing every mutation site would be a list to keep in sync forever, and one omission is a silent loss. Persistence also **coalesces**: it was fire-and-forget with no in-flight guard, so two stores could overlap on an unguarded `UPDATE` and land out of order, the older winning; and a store's completion could clear the dirty flag against an edit that arrived _during_ the write, swallowing it until the next unrelated block edit. Now one store runs at a time with at most one follow-up queued, the flag is cleared against the snapshot actually taken, and a failed write re-marks the room dirty to retry rather than dropping the state.

fix(online): validate world creation input and enforce the profile cap

createWorld checked the name, the kind, and that the seed was finite,
then trusted the rest — and the route handed it a bare-cast JSON body. So
a hand-rolled POST /api/worlds could:

- set worldType/gameMode/difficulty to anything (the columns are plain
  text with no DB enum, and server/room.ts casts them into GameEngine at
  room boot — worldgen then ran on a value it never expected),
- send a seed past int4 (Number.isFinite(1e20) is true; the insert then
  overflowed the integer column into an unhandled 500 instead of a 400),
- set a non-string name that threw on .trim() — again a 500, not a 400.

Each field is now validated against the SAME is-guards the client
already uses (isWorldType/isGameMode/isDifficulty, lib/game/worlds.ts),
the seed is bounded to the column's range, and name/hardcore are
type-checked. The route stays a thin cast: createWorld is the validation
boundary and now treats every field as untrusted.

Also closes a quota bypass. MAX_WORLDS_PER_PROFILE was enforced only
`if (input.profileId)`, so omitting it created uncapped, profile-less
rows. An mp world is always profile-scoped in the UI (OnlineWorldSelect
always sends one), so it now requires a profileId — while sp-cloud
legitimately omits it, because uploads from the local menus are
account-level. That asymmetry (unlike the unconditional
MAX_ONLINE_PROFILES cap) was the hole.

Test helper updated: makeWorld now creates a profile for mp worlds, which
is the path production takes. Nothing legitimate changes — the real
client always sent valid values.

content.text: Now I understand `acceptInvite` fully. Two real bugs the review found: the consume and the membership insert aren't in one transaction (a failed insert burns a use forever), and two concurrent same-user accepts both pass the `existing` check and both consume, but `onConflictDoNothing` yields one membership — so 2 uses for 1 member. The fix: insert membership *first* (which atomically dedupes concurrent same-user accepts), consume only when the insert created a row, in one transaction.

lines: ### Fixed

+- **Invite acceptance is now transactional, and resync requests are rate-limited**: two smaller online-server fixes. Accepting an invite consumed a use and then inserted the membership as two separate statements, so a failed insert burned a use with nothing to show for it, and two accepts from the _same_ user racing each other both passed a read-side "already a member?" check and each consumed a use — leaving two uses spent for the one membership the unique index actually created. The membership insert now goes first inside a transaction: concurrent same-user accepts dedupe on the index (the loser consumes nothing), and a use is spent if and only if a membership is granted. Separately, the `resync` message — which serializes and gzips a room's entire world diff — had no rate limit, so a hand-rolled client could loop it and stack full-world gzips against the 20 Hz tick loop every room in the process shares; it's now budgeted per second like the `cmd`/`chat`/`attack` messages. (No legitimate client sends `resync` in a loop; both are hardening against a crafted one.)

- **`POST /api/worlds` validates its body instead of trusting it**: the create-world handler cast the request JSON straight to its input type and passed it on, and the service checked only the name, kind, and that the seed was finite. So a hand-rolled request could set `worldType`/`gameMode`/`difficulty` to anything — the columns have no DB-level enum and the game server casts them straight into the engine at room boot — send a seed past int4 (a Postgres overflow surfaced as a 500, not a clean rejection), or set a non-string name that threw on `.trim()`. It now validates each field through the same `isWorldType`/`isGameMode`/`isDifficulty` guards the client already uses, bounds the seed to the column's range, and type-checks the rest. It also closes a **quota bypass**: `MAX_WORLDS_PER_PROFILE` was only checked when a `profileId` was supplied, so omitting it created uncapped, profile-less worlds — `mp` worlds (always profile-scoped in the UI) now require one, while `sp-cloud` stays account-level for the upload path. Nothing legitimate changes; the real client always sent valid values.

- **A brief network blip in an online world reconnects cleanly instead of sometimes killing the session**: the client's socket-close handling wasn't idempotent. A browser fires **both** `error` and `close` for an abnormal drop, and both ran the same close path — so one blip scheduled two reconnects, burned two rungs of the back-off ladder, minted two tickets, and raced two handshakes. The second handshake's join then kicked the first connection (`CLOSE_KICKED`, a fatal code), and because that orphaned socket's handlers were still bound, its close drove the session that had _just reconnected_ straight to "disconnected". A transient blip could therefore take down a session that had already recovered. Each socket now carries a connection generation: a close is acted on only for the live generation (a superseded socket's late close is ignored), and acting on one advances the generation so the same socket's error+close pair schedules exactly one reconnect. The reconnect timer is also single — a new rung clears any pending one rather than orphaning it. (Networking-only; no protocol or save change.)

- **Rejoining a world just as it's evicted can no longer resurrect it from stale state**: an idle room was dropped from the registry _before_ its shutdown finished persisting, and that final write is a whole-world gzip plus a Postgres round-trip — a window wide enough to land in. A join arriving inside it found no room, took the load path, and read the blob the shutdown was still in the middle of replacing. The process then held **two** `Room` objects for one world, both writing the same row through an `UPDATE` with no version guard: last write wins, and the eviction's is typically the older one, so the evicted room's final state — the last minutes before it emptied — silently lost. Eviction now hands the room from "live" to "closing" in one step: it leaves the registry (nobody may join a room that's closing its sockets) and a load for that world waits for the shutdown's write to land before reading the row, so it can only ever build a room from post-shutdown state.

acceptInvite consumed a use and inserted the membership as two separate

problems:

- Two accepts from the SAME user racing both passed the read-side check
  (neither had inserted yet) and each consumed a use, while
  onConflictDoNothing created just one membership. Net: two uses spent
  for one member, contradicting the "each NEW membership consumes one
  use" contract.

Both close by moving the membership insert FIRST, inside a transaction.
The insert dedupes concurrent same-user accepts on the unique index (the
loser gets zero rows back and consumes nothing), and the use is consumed
only when a row was actually inserted. If the invite ran out between the
resolve and the consume, the transaction aborts and the membership rolls
back with it — a use is spent iff a membership is granted. Expiry joined
the consume predicate too, closing the ms-wide TOCTOU against
resolveInvite.

The `resync` handler serializes and gzips a room's entire world diff and
had no rate limit — and Bun doesn't serialize a socket's concurrent
message handlers, so a hand-rolled client looping it stacks full-world
gzips against the 20 Hz tick loop every room in the process shares. It's
now budgeted per second (RESYNC_PER_SECOND = 3) alongside the existing
cmd/chat/attack budgets, refilled at the same second-boundary reset. No
real client loops resync; this is hardening against a crafted one.

The concurrent-accept test fails against the old consume-then-insert
code (it reproduces the double-consume), so it's a real regression, not
just characterization.
